Recall what each level means for one chain: secondary is local coiling like alpha-helix, tertiary is the whole 3D folding of that one chain, quaternary needs two or more chains together.
walkthrough:
**Spot the Number of Polypeptides**

Look at the question stem. It tells you this is a polypeptide, singular. That is one chain only.

That one detail already rules out a lot. Quaternary structure always involves more than one polypeptide chain interacting.

**Recall Secondary vs Tertiary**

Secondary structure is just local folding, like an alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet held by hydrogen bonds.

Tertiary structure is the further folding and coiling of that whole single chain into its complete 3D shape.

**Apply It to the Diagram**

The diagram shows a loose spiral in the middle plus tightly coiled tangled regions at the ends. Together they make up the overall 3D shape of this one chain.

So we are not just describing the spiral alone, we are describing the whole folded molecule. That is tertiary structure, so D is correct.

options.A: Not quaternary. Quaternary needs two or more polypeptides, but here we have only one polypeptide.
options.B: Not quaternary for the same reason. Having different shaped regions in one chain does not make it quaternary.
options.C: The loose spiral is a secondary feature, but the question asks about the whole molecule with all its regions folded into a 3D shape, which is tertiary.
options.D: Correct. The folding of a single polypeptide chain, including its spiral and tightly coiled regions, into an overall 3D shape is tertiary structure.
